about me

A little more context

I graduated from ESSEC Business School with a Global BBA (Paris & Singapore), ranked #1 in France. I spent a semester at WU Vienna, and along the way I've worked on brand-building, product development, and CSR strategy across three countries.

What actually gets me excited is the moment a brand idea turns into something real — a product on a shelf, a campaign that lands, a stakeholder who says yes. I've done that as a co-founder, as an intern inside a Nestlé CSR team, and as a product developer designing bags for U.S. and E.U. export markets.

I'm looking for a full-time role in brand strategy and marketing — moving to Paris, and bring that same hands-on energy to a bigger stage.

academic research

The Business of Indian Weddings

My ESSEC dissertation — mixed-methods research on why Indian wedding spending defies the logic you'd expect. 77 survey respondents, 7 in-depth interviews across Kolkata, Delhi, and London.

$103.93B
Industry value in 2024, projected $200B+ by 2030
100%
of interviewees said family — not the couple — made final spending calls
₹15.5L
average wedding loan size in 2025; 15.2% borrowed formally
Where the money actually goes
Survey of 77 respondents — expenditure breakdown by category
Venue & Catering 34%
Clothing & Styling 21%
Jewellery 18%
Photography/Video 12%
Décor 9%
Other 6%
Key insight: Venue + jewellery alone account for over half of all spending — both are heavily family-driven categories.
Indian Wedding Consumption Pyramid
A conceptual framework I developed for this dissertation — hover each tier
Personal Identity
Couple's self-expression & aesthetics
Digital Aspiration
Social media, influencers, global aesthetics
Emotional Value
Jewellery, rituals — non-negotiable symbolic spend
Social Visibility
Status display, community expectations
Cultural Obligation
Family authority — the dominant driver
01 Family authority rules ⌄
All 7 interview participants — regardless of religion, age, or profession — confirmed family as the ultimate financial and social authority. Family approval ranked above personal preference AND social media influence for every major expenditure category.
"Final decision mummy-papa ka hi hota tha." — Bride-to-be, age 23, Kolkata
02 Digital aspiration is real, but limited ⌄
Instagram and Pinterest drive aspiration in décor, photography, and styling — over 50% of vendor bookings now happen via online platforms. But family retains normative control over high-stakes categories like jewellery. Social media tells people what they want; family decides what they do.
03 Symbolic categories are protected ⌄
Jewellery and ceremonial rituals are exempt from the cost-cutting logic applied everywhere else. Interviewees described jewellery as having "long-term symbolic value" — it's viewed as an heirloom, not an expenditure, and treated as a family obligation rather than a purchase decision.
04 Income vs. spending is non-linear ⌄
Wedding debt concentrates in the aspirational middle class — not the very poor or very rich. Spending is governed by community thresholds, not household income: lower income sees a proportionally high social floor, middle income carries the highest debt burden, and upper income plateaus once the status signal is already sent.

group project — essec

Onitsuka Tiger: Premium to Luxury

A brand repositioning strategy with two teammates, taking Onitsuka Tiger from a premium streetwear label to a genuine luxury house. Click a channel to see the campaign concept.

The core idea: luxury communicates by saying less. Never show a price. Never run a sale. Never use influencers. So we built a communication strategy on scarcity of content instead of abundance — one voice, six channels, all built around a single story: Kobe, 1949.
▶
Hero Film
"The Hands of Kobe"
A 3-minute silent documentary. Click to see the concept.
No voiceover — only the sounds of leather and tools. The artisan's face is never shown, only hands. History is the hero.

Open: Close-up of leather pressed flat, dawn light, Kobe factory.
Middle: Hand-lasting a sole in real time, no cuts for 45 seconds.
End: Shoe placed in a paulownia box. Lid closed. Text: "Kobe, 1949."
Cinema → YouTube → Flagship screens
◎
30-Sec Spot
"Silence is a Language"
A young artist sketches on a street corner. Click to see the concept.
A young artist sketches in silence on a street corner, wearing Onitsuka Tiger shoes. People of every nationality move through the same streets. Each pencil stroke mirrors the rhythm of footsteps on the pavement. Zero dialogue — the global metropolis is the character.

"Some observe it. Some move with it." Every execution follows one rule: the product is the detail, never the subject.
TV broadcast → Digital pre-roll
▪
Print Campaign
"Kobe, 1949"
Real archival photographs. Click to see the concept.
Real archival photographs of Kobe from 1949–65 — port workers, fishermen, children running. The shoe appears barely visible in one corner. Once seen, it cannot be unseen. No tagline, no product shot.

A companion series, "One Stitch," runs billboards showing only 1cm² of the shoe at extreme macro: a stitch, a seam, a curve of sole.
Vogue Japan · Monocle · Wallpaper · AnOther
◻
Instagram
Ghost Presence — 12 images only
Delete all promotional posts. Click to see the concept.
The account becomes a gallery of exactly 12 images, changed once a year. No captions beyond "Kobe, 1949." No hashtags, no geotags, no links, no stories, no reels, no DMs acknowledged.

Scarcity of content is the luxury signal — the opposite of the brand's current 889K-follower, high-frequency posting strategy.
Delete everything to say more
◆
Print Journal
"Katachi" (形) Art Journal
A bi-annual journal about form and craft. Click to see the concept.
An art journal about form, craft, and the things that endure — bi-annual, with essays by Japanese architects, chefs, and ceramicists, never marketers. Zero product placement; the brand is the editorial quality itself.

Distributed only inside flagships and select 5-star hotel concierges — no digital version exists.
Aman · Rosewood · Mandarin Oriental
●
Experiential
"The Kobe Room"
A single room recreating the 1949 factory. Click to see the concept.
A single room recreating the 1949 Kobe factory — leather smell, tools, archival photos on every wall. Installed for 72 hours in 5 cities. Invitation only, 10 guests per hour, no photography allowed. The room is the advertisement.
Paris · Milan · Tokyo · New York · Singapore
